Introduction
Federal and state laws regulating the use of cannabinoid products containing Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) have changed substantially over the past decade. A number of states have legalized medical and non-medical use of THC-containing products, i.e., cannabis, and the 2018 Farm Bill broadly legalized the production and sales of CBD products, i.e., the hemp-derived products that contain no more than 0.3% THC, by removing them from Schedule I status under the Controlled Substances Act (Hudak, 2018). In the increasingly permissive environment for cannabinoid use, commercial markets for and sales of THC and CBD products, including oils/tinctures, topical preparations/serums, edibles/drinks, capsules/pills, and concentrates, have proliferated for their purported therapeutic benefits and as dietary supplements (Spindle et al., 2019; Skodzinski, 2024; Wagoner et al., 2021).
Systematic reviews of the therapeutic benefits of THC-dominant cannabinoid products showed low to moderate evidence for small improvements in chronic and neuropathic pain but increased risk for dizziness and sedation (Chou et al., 2023; McDonagh et al., 2022; Seffah et al., 2023). Medicinal cannabis does not yet have an established evidence base for its benefits for mental illnesses (Crichton et al., 2024; Seffah et al., 2023; Stanciu et al., 2021) and dementia (Bosnjak Kuharic et al., 2021). Moreover, systematic reviews found that cannabis use is associated with the development and worsened course and prognosis of major depressive and bipolar disorders (Sorkhou et al., 2024; Tourjman et al., 2023). Although dronabinol (whose trade names include Marinol and Syndros) was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1985 for treatment of nausea and vomiting associated with cancer chemotherapy and low appetite among people diagnosed with AIDS, a systematic review found THC not to have positive effects on appetite-related symptoms in cancer patients (National Cancer Institute, 2023; Razmovski-Naumovski et al., 2022).
Despite its purported health and wellness benefits, scientific evidence for CBD is also slim except for its efficacy and safety in pediatric patients with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome or Dravet syndrome: rare and severe forms of epilepsy with onset in early childhood (Aderinto et al., 2024; Lattanzi et al., 2019; Laux et al., 2019). Epidiolex for Lennox-Gastaut and Dravet syndromes is the only FDA-approved CBD-based prescription medicine. Research on CBD’s other therapeutic benefits is in its incipient stage, and the outcomes of limited clinical trials showed little or no positive medicinal effects for different types of pain (Filippini et al., 2022; Häuser et al., 2023; Mücke et al., 2018) or mental health problems (Dammann et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2020; Kirkland et al., 2022). However, unlike psychoactive THC, CBD has been shown to be safe except for short-term sedation, drowsiness, or some cognitive delays as side effects in some individuals (Lo et al., 2024; Manning et al., 2024; MacNair et al., 2022).
The lack of scientific evidence of positive health effects and the FDA’s clear warnings about unproven health claims made by manufacturers selling CBD products over the counter did not stop the rapid uptake of CBD (Soleymanpour et al., 2021; Wagoner et al., 2021). In 2019, 14% of U.S. adults tried CBD (Sideris & Doan, 2024). In the 2022 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), 23% and 20% of the adult (age ≥ 18 years) population self-reported past-year use of cannabis and CBD, respectively; more than half of cannabis users co-used CBD and close to two-thirds of CBD users co-used cannabis (Choi et al., 2024). The high prevalence of CBD-cannabis co-use is likely because users of either product tend to have more positive perceptions leading to higher inclination to use the other (Spinella et al., 2023). In their study of Canadian adults, Spinella et al. found that both prior cannabis users and nonusers rated CBD higher than THC in therapeutic effects on sleep, stress, pain, anxiety, attention, and nausea. Compared to nonusers, prior cannabis users also rated all cannabinoids higher for many non-therapeutic positive effects including enhanced mood, creativity, and social and sexual facilitation, and were less likely to endorse negative effects including the risks for impaired cognition, addiction, and psychosis. CBD users mostly report high perceived positive health and wellness effects (Binkowska et al., 2024; Corroon & Phillips, 2018; Fedorova et al., 2021; Geppert et al., 2023; Goodman et al., 2022; Kaufman et al., 2023; Leas et al., 2020; Moltke & Hindocha, 2021).
Cannabinoid use has been increasing among adults of all ages (Caulkins, 2024; Wilson-Poe et al., 2023); however, the increases were fastest among those age 50 and older (Han & Palamar, 2020). Individuals age 50 and older also compose the largest share of state medical cannabis registrants, with chronic pain, musculoskeletal disorders and spasms, cancer, Parkinson’s disease, and sleep disorders being the primary conditions for medicinal use (Brown et al., 2020; Kaufmann et al., 2022; Porter et al., 2021). These studies showed that a majority of medical users, especially those age 65 and older, used CBD-only or CBD-dominant (i.e., high CBD to THC ratio) products. Given its purported health and wellness benefits and higher safety evidence than THC, it is not surprising that older adults (age 65+) who tend to have more health-related problems are attracted to using CBD. They may be especially inclined to use CBD only or CBD+THC as opposed to THC-only products to reduce potential harms associated with THC-only use. A systematic review found that CBD may reduce intense experiences of anxiety or psychosis-like effects, but not subjective intoxication or psychomotor effects, of THC (Freeman et al., 2019). A study also found that regular cannabis users who consumed a THC+CBD product reported similar levels of positive and psychotomimetic effects relative to those who consumed a THC-only product, despite consuming less THC and displaying lower plasma THC concentrations (Gibson et al., 2024).
Older adults may also want to substitute CBD for opioids and other pain medications (Boehnke et al., 2021). A survey of medical cannabis dispensary members (ages 18–84) showed that three quarters reduced their use of opioids and two thirds reduced anti-anxiety, migraine, and sleep medications and more than one-third reduced anti-depressant use (Piper et al., 2017). A 4-week observational study of CBD users (ages 18–75) also found that among those who took CBD for chronic pain, 42% and 24% decreased or stopped over-the-counter and prescription drugs, respectively, during the study period (Kaufmann et al., 2023). Those who used CBD for sleep disorders, mental health problems, and other conditions also reduced or stopped over-the-counter (25–33%) and prescription (8–23%) drugs (Kaufmann et al., 2023).
To date, however, little epidemiologic research has been done on CBD use among those age 50 years and older. In the present study, we used the 2022 NSDUH (that included the questions about past-year and past-month use of “CBD or hemp products made from hemp plants” (referred to as CBD hereafter for brevity) for the first time in the annual NSDUH history) and examined the prevalence of past-year CBD and cannabis use among individuals age 50 and older and the associations of CBD use with medical or non-medical cannabis use, physical and mental health statuses, and other substance use, controlling for sociodemographic factors.
Given the significant differences in physical and mental health and substance use statuses between the 50–64 age group and the 65+ age group, especially among cannabis users (Yang et al., 2024), we examined these two age groups separately. Yang et al. found that of the two age groups of cannabis users, the 65+ age group had a higher prevalence of more cardiovascular and musculoskeletal diseases, but the 50–64 age group had a higher prevalence of mood and anxiety disorders and alcohol and tobacco use disorders. Thus, CBD use may be associated with both physical and mental health problems in the 50–64 age group and with physical health problems in the 65+ age group. The study hypotheses were that: (H1) in both age groups, both medical and non-medical cannabis use would be significantly positively associated with CBD use; (H2a) moderate/severe mental illness and other substance use, as well as physical health problems, would be significantly positively associated with CBD use in the 50–64 age group; and (H2b) physical health problems will be significantly positively associated with CBD use in the 65+ age group. The findings will provide valuable insight into the associations between cannabis and CBD use and the physical and mental health and other substance use characteristics of individuals age 50 and older who used CBD as well as any potential differences between the 50–64 and the 65+ age groups.
Methods
Data source
The NSDUH is an annual epidemiologic survey, funded by the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), of the civilian, non-institutionalized, age 12+ population to measure the prevalence of substance use, mental and substance use disorders, behavioral health treatment, and physical/functional health and healthcare use. Because of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, data collection in 2022 was done using both in-person and online modes. However, starting February 3, 2022, in-person data collection was available in all states and counties, and in-person data collection commenced after potential respondents were first given the opportunity to complete the survey online. The overall percentage of interviews completed online was 40.7% for 2022 (Center for Behavioral Statistics and Quality, 2023). The 2022 NSDUH public use data set includes responses from 59,069 individuals who completed an in-person or web-based NSDUH survey. Of these, 11,969 were age 12–17, and 47,100 were age 18 years or older (adults). In this study, we focused on 10,560 respondents, representing nearly 119 million U.S. adults, who were age 50 and older. Analysis of these de-identified public-use data was exempt from the authors’ institutional review boards’ review.
Measures
CBD and cannabis use: In the 2022 NSDUH, respondents were asked two questions about “CBD or hemp products made from hemp plants”: (1) Ever use, even once, of any CBD or hemp products (yes or no); and (2) time since the last use of any form of CBD or hemp product (within the past 30 days, more than 30 days ago but within the past 12 months, and more than 12 months ago). Respondents were also asked about use and time since the last use of “marijuana or any cannabis product, sometimes called pot, weed, hashish, or concentrates, excluding CBD or hemp products.” Based on the responses to these questions, we created the past-year CBD and cannabis use variables (nonuse of CBD or cannabis, CBD use only, cannabis use only, both CBD and cannabis use). Cannabis users were also asked about medical use (no vs. any medical use), frequency of use (in number of days), and the questions pertaining to the 11 criteria for DSM-5 cannabis use disorder (CUD). The NSDUH data set provided the summary variables for CUD (yes or no) and CUD severity (mild [2–3 symptoms], moderate [4–5 symptoms], or severe [6–11 symptoms]) (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
Physical and mental health and other substance use: Physical health status was measured with the number (0–10) of diagnosed chronic illnesses, including asthma, cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, heart disease, hepatitis, HIV/AIDS, hypertension, kidney disease, and liver disease. Mental health status was measured with any past-year mental illness (none, mild, moderate, serious). Serious mental illness refers to any mental, behavioral, or emotional disorder--excluding developmental and substance use disorders--that substantially interfered with or limited one or more major life activities (SAMHSA, 2023). Past-year other substance use problems included in the study were nicotine dependence (Heatherton, et al., 1991), DSM-5 alcohol use disorder, any prescription opioid, tranquillizer, and/or sedative medication use disorder (referred to as disordered psychotherapeutic drug use hereafter), and the use of any illicit drugs excluding cannabis.
Sociodemographic factors were age (50–64 and 65+ years); gender; race/ethnicity; marital status (married vs. not married); education (college degree vs. no college degree); income (<poverty line, up to 2X poverty line, >2X poverty line); and the residence in a medical cannabis legal state (yes vs. no).
Analysis
We used Stata/MP 18’s svy function (College Station, TX) and subpop command in all analyses to account for NSDUH’s multi-stage, stratified sampling estimates to ensure that variance estimates incorporate the full sampling design. All estimates presented in this study are weighted except sample sizes. First, we calculated the prevalence, with 95% confidence intervals (CI), of past-year CBD and cannabis use in the 50–64 and the 65+ age groups. Second, we used Pearson’s χ2 and t tests to compare CBD users with nonusers in the 50–64 and the 65+ age groups regarding cannabis use, sociodemographic, physical and mental health, and other substance use characteristics. Third, we fitted three generalized linear models (GLMs) for a Poisson distribution with a log link function to test the study hypotheses (associations of CBD use with cannabis use [medical and non-medical uses vs. no cannabis use), physical and mental health statues, and other substance use) for the combined age group (i.e., all those age 50 and older, to examine age group effect) and separately for the 50–64 age and 65+ age groups. We further examined possible differences between medical versus nonmedical uses of cannabis in their associations with CBD use by fitting two additional GLMs (one for each age group) with non-medical use as the reference category (i.e., medical cannabis use and nonuse of cannabis vs. non-medical use of cannabis). The GLM results are presented as incidence rate ratios (IRR) with 95% CI. We used the Poisson distribution with a log link rather than logistic regression models because odds ratios exaggerate the true relative risk to some degree when the event (i.e., CBD use) is a common (i.e., >10%) occurrence (Grimes & Schulz, 2008). As a preliminary diagnostic, variance inflation factor (VIF), using a cut-off of 2.50 (Allison, 2012), from linear regression models was used to assess multicollinearity among covariates. VIF diagnostics indicated that multicollinearity was not a concern. Significance was set at p<.05.
Results
Prevalence of past-year CBD and cannabis use in the 50–64 and 65+ age groups
Table 1 shows that 18.3% and 14.3% of the 50–64 and 65+ age groups, respectively, reported using CBD in the preceding 12 months. The corresponding percentages for cannabis use were 18.0% and 8.0%, showing that CBD use was more prevalent than cannabis use in the 65+ age group. Table 1 also shows that 8.9% and 9.9% of the 50–64 and the 65+ age groups, respectively, reported using CBD alone; 8.6% and 3.6%, respectively, reported using cannabis alone; and 9.4% and 4.4%, respectively, reported using both CBD and cannabis.
Characteristics of CBD users compared to nonusers
Table 2 shows that in the 50–64 age group, 51.3% of CBD users, compared to 10.6% of nonusers of CBD, used cannabis. In the 65+ age group, 30.7% of CBD users, compared to 4.3% of nonusers of CBD used cannabis. Of the CBD-cannabis co-users, 22.4% and 29.0% in the 50–64 and 65+ age groups, respectively, were medical cannabis users. In both age groups, CBD users also had higher proportions of non-Hispanic whites. In the 50–64 age group, CBD users had a higher proportion of females than non-users. In the 65+ age group, CBD users included higher proportions of college graduates and the residents of medical cannabis legal states.
Among CBD users, 10.8% of the 50–64 age group had CUD (7.6% mild, 1.9% moderate, and 1.3% severe CUDs); and 2.5% of the 65+ age group had CUD (1.6% mild and 0.9% moderate CUDs). Among nonusers of CBD, 1.9% and 0.3% of the 50–64 and 65+ age groups, respectively, had CUD. Additional analyses showed that among cannabis users age 50–64 (n=877), CBD users and nonusers did not differ on CUD rates (F[2.87, 143.68]=0.360, p=.773), although a larger proportion of CBD users (58.2% vs. 41.1%) used cannabis more frequently (i.e., 100+ days; F[3.76, 188.04]=2.857, p=.028). Among cannabis users age 65+ (n=429), CBD users and non-users did not differ on CUD rates (F[1.67, 80.21]=0.272, p=.723) and cannabis use frequency (42.5% vs. 43.5% used 100+ days; F[3.09, 148.41]=0.802, p=.498).
Table 2 also shows that CBD users in the age 50–64 age group had higher rates of chronic illnesses, any mental illnesses, alcohol use disorder, nicotine dependence, and illicit drugs. CBD users in the 65+ age group included higher rates of any mental illness, alcohol use disorder, disordered psychotherapeutic drug use, and illicit drug use.
Correlates of past-year CBD use: Results from GLMs
The second column of Table 3 shows that age group (65+ years vs. 50–64 years) was not a significant factor for CBD use when other variables were controlled for. The third and fourth columns of Table 3 shows that in both age groups, CBD use was significantly associated with both medical and non-medical cannabis use: IRR=5.17, 95% CI=4.07–6.57 for any medical use and IRR=4.42, 95% CI=3.65–5.37 for non-medical use in the 50–64 age group; and IRR=5.59, 95% CI=4.36–7.18 for any medical use and IRR=4.19, 95% CI=3.18–5.54 for nonmedical use in the 65+ age group. These findings support H1.
Figure 1 is the graphic illustration of the GLM results shown in Table 3 regarding the associations between CBD use and cannabis use after adjusting for all other covariates.
Additional analyses (results not included in Table 3) showed that medical or non-medical use did not differ significantly in the 50–64 age group (IRR=1.17, 95% CI=0.94–1.45, p=.150); however, in the 65+ age group, the likelihood of CBD use was higher among medical cannabis users than among non-medical users (IRR=1.33, 95% CI=1.02–1.74, p=.033).
In the 50–64 age group, CBD use was also significantly associated with the number of chronic illnesses (IRR=1.13, 95% CI=1.05–1.22), any mental illness (IRR=1.29, 95% CI=1.02–1.62 for mild mental illness and IRR=1.35, 95% CI=1.03–1.77 for moderate/severe mental illness), and illicit drug use (IRR=1.30, 95% CI=1.07–1.57). In the 65+ age group, CBD use was significantly associated with disordered psychotherapeutic drug use (IRR=1.50, 95% CI=1.05–2.14). These findings support H2a but not H2b.
Of the sociodemographic factors, the likelihood of CBD use in the 50–64 age group was higher among females than males, married than non-married individuals, and non-Hispanic whites than Blacks, Hispanics, and other racial/ethnic groups. In the 65+ age group, the likelihood of CBD use was lower among Hispanics but higher among the residents of medical cannabis legal states.
Discussion
This study is the first examination of nationally representative, epidemiologic data on CBD use among U.S. individuals age 50 and older. The findings show that the prevalence of past-year CBD use in the 50–64 age group (18.3%) was similar to that of cannabis use (18.0%) in 2022. However, the prevalence of CBD use in the 65+ age group was significantly higher than that of cannabis use (14.3% vs. 8.0%), indicating that CBD uptake has even outpaced that of rapidly-increasing cannabis use in this age group. title: Cannabis use and neurocognitive performance at 13-14 Years-Old: Optimizing assessment with hair toxicology in the Adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) study.
abstract: Cannabis is widely used, including in early adolescence, with prevalence rates varying by measurement method (e.g., toxicology vs. self-report). Critical neurocognitive development occurs throughout adolescence. Given conflicting prior brain-behavior results in cannabis research, improved measurement of cannabis use in younger adolescents is needed. Data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study Year 4 follow-up (participant age: 13-14 years-old) included hair samples assessed by LC-MS/MS and GC-MS/MS, quantifying THCCOOH (THC metabolite), THC, and cannabidiol concentrations, and the NIH Toolbox Cognitive Battery. Youth whose hair was positive for cannabinoids or reported past-year cannabis use were included in a Cannabis Use (CU) group (n = 123) and matched with non-using Controls on sociodemographics (n = 123). Standard and nested ANCOVAs assessed group status predicting cognitive performance, controlling for family relationships. Follow-up correlations assessed cannabinoid hair concentration, self-reported cannabis use, and neurocognition. CU scored lower on Picture Memory (p = .03) than Controls. Within the CU group, THCCOOH negatively correlated with Picture Vocabulary (r = -0.20, p = .03) and Flanker Inhibitory Control and Attention (r = -0.19, p = .04), and past-year cannabis use was negatively associated with List Sorting Working Memory (r = -0.33, p = .0002) and Picture Sequence Memory (r = -0.19, p = .04) performances. Youth who had used cannabis showed lower scores on an episodic memory task, and more cannabis use was linked to poorer performances on verbal, inhibitory, working memory, and episodic memory tasks. Combining hair toxicology with self-report revealed more brain-behavior relationships than self-report data alone. These youth will be followed to determine long-term substance use and neurocognition trajectories.

Introduction
In recent decades, cannabis use changed worldwide, including legal status, increased potency (Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol [THC] concentration) (ElSohly et al., 2021; ElSohly et al., 2016), and methods of use (e. g., dabs, edibles, vaped flower) (Meacham et al., 2018), while high levels of use by adolescents and young adults remained relatively stable (Patrick et al., 2022; Schulenberg et al., 2018). There are over 120 cannabinoid constituents (ElSohly et al., 2017), with THC and cannabidiol (CBD) the best known and researched. THC acts as a partial agonist of the endocannabinoid system (ECS) binding to cannabinoid 1 (CB1) and CB2 receptors, while CBD is an allosteric modulator at the CB1 receptor indirectly affecting ECS activity (McPartland et al., 2015; Pertwee, 2008). Preliminary evidence suggests that THC in particular disrupts CB1 receptor signaling, which may in turn impact cognitive functioning (Mizrahi et al., 2017). Adolescence marks a critical period of neuroanatomical and cognitive development (Giedd et al., 2015; Gogtay et al., 2004; Shaw et al., 2008), including within the ECS system (Schneider, 2008), in which teenagers may be particularly vulnerable to exposure to exogenous cannabinoids. Yet there are conflicting findings regarding cognitive effects of repeated cannabis use in adolescents and young adults. Some authors argue that cannabis use has no impact on cognition beyond 72 hours after use (Scott et al., 2018), indicating the need for more fine-grained detail, such as objective measurement of cannabis exposure, to clarify the relationship between cannabis and cognition in the developing brain. Further, cannabis and cognition are limitedly studied in early adolescence.
Several preliminary studies of hair analyses for cannabinoid content reveal that cannabinoid analytes in hair may reveal unique and important relationships in cannabis-using adults. One suggests THC concentration in hair relates to cognitive and psychiatric functioning (Morgan et al., 2012). Another study found cannabinoid concentrations in hair corresponded to psychiatric symptoms, such as hallucinations in adults < 35 years-old (Nestoros et al., 2017). More recently, a study did not find cannabinoids in hair to significantly improve a predictive model of acute psychotic symptoms, despite significant correlations between symptoms and THC and CBD hair concentrations (Curran et al., 2019). Larger hippocampal volumes were found when THC and CBD were present in hair compared to THC alone (Demirakca et al., 2011; Yucel et al., 2016), perhaps because CBD may modulate THC metabolism (Greene et al., 2018).
Hair analyses detect THC, THC’s inactive metabolite (THCCOOH), and CBD in hair. Presence of each analyte can indicate cannabis use, though detection may vary for a variety of reasons. For example, parent analytes present in cannabis smoke (i.e., THC or CBD) typically have higher concentrations than metabolites, except in cases of oral ingestion (e.g., edibles) (Huestis et al., 2007). THCCOOH is also the definitive indicator of actual cannabis use rather than potential external contamination from cannabis smoke (Hill et al., 2016). If quantitative hair cannabinoid concentrations relate to cognitive performance, cannabinoid concentrations may explain some discrepancies in neurocognitive performance and other outcomes (Gonzalez et al., 2017; Lisdahl et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2018), suggesting cannabinoid analyte concentrations in hair may be better markers to assess the impact of cannabis than relying on self-report alone. Yet studies thus far are limited to adults who regularly use cannabis, despite the fact that youth may be more vulnerable to cannabis effects.
On balance, cannabinoid content from hair alone may not be enough to identify all youth who use cannabis, particularly during early adolescence (Wade et al., 2023). Moderate to frequent episodes of cannabis use are often needed for detection in hair (Huestis et al., 2007; Taylor et al., 2017), which is more frequent than most youth experimentation (Sullivan et al., 2022). Thus, combining hair cannabinoid results with self-reported cannabis use may be the most appropriate means of identifying all youth who use cannabis (Wade et al., 2023), optimizing power for detecting correlates of use.
Here, we investigate the presence of cannabinoids in hair and self-reported cannabis use in relation to neurocognitive performance in early adolescence. We leverage the large, diverse Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, wherein around 10 % of participants (~1,200) have their hair assayed on an annual basis (Lisdahl et al., 2018; Wade et al., 2023; Wade et al., 2022), in addition to undergoing a full cognitive assessment every other year. We first combine self-reported cannabis use with objective hair toxicology from the Year 4 annual follow-up visit to identify adolescent cannabis users. We next match youth with cannabis use to non-using controls on sociodemographic characteristics and compare group performance on neurocognitive measures. Then, given the potential for dose-dependent relationships between cannabinoids and cognition, we explore whether THC, THCCOOH, and/or CBD concentrations and self-reported standard units of use relate to neurocognitive performance.
Materials and methods
Data were derived from the 21-site, longitudinal ABCD Study. Nearly 12,000 youth were initially enrolled at ages 9–10 years and are followed annually through adolescence. In data release 5.0 (June 2023; https://doi.org/10.15154/8873-zj65), 24,925 had hair samples, with 2,971 analyzed (approximately 90% of whom were at high risk of substance use; for details, see Wade et al., 2023; Wade et al., 2022). Of participants with hair analysis results at Year 4 follow-up (n = 601 out of 2,067 collected samples, ages 13–14 years), 123 were classified as youth with cannabis use (CU): 54 had cannabinoids present in hair, 32 self-reported cannabis use (at least a puff) in the past year, and 37 had cannabinoids present in hair and self-reported cannabis use in the past year. These 123 CU were matched with 123 non-using controls, for a total sample size of n = 246; all included participants were required to have neurocognitive data on at least one task. Data were collected between September 2020 and January 2022, and all participants completed at least part of their visit in person to provide a hair sample. Though longitudinal data from the ABCD cohort are available, repeat hair analysis data within the same participant are limited, precluding use of the same cannabis use identification methods; thus, analyses were limited to Year 4 follow-up. Participants and their parents/guardians provided written informed assent and consent. The UCSD Institutional Review Board approved all aspects of this study.
Participant matching.
Participants with cannabis use were matched on age, sex at birth, race/ethnicity, and socioeconomic factors (parental education and household income) to those with tested hair samples and no indication of cannabis use with the R package MatchIt (Ho et al., 2011). Matched control participants were required to have no indication of past-year cannabis use based on self-report, parent report, and hair results. Matches were fair based on relatively low standard mean difference (around or below 0.1 on each variable, with the largest variability in race/ethnicity variables) and empirical cumulative distribution functions close to 0 on all variables.
Measures
Sociodemographic and hair characteristics.
Parents reported youth sex at birth, household income, race, ethnicity, and highest parental education at baseline (Barch et al., 2018), and age was recorded at the time of hair collection. Siblings are enrolled in the ABCD Study, and 14 sibling pairs (n = 28 participants) were included in the present analyses; each participant has a family ID that is either unique if they do not have a sibling in the study or shared with their sibling, if they also participate in the ABCD Study. Youth who used cannabis (identified by hair or self-report) were matched to nonusers (denied cannabis use on self-report; no positive hair for any substances).
Self-Reported substance use.
After reminding participants of the confidential nature of their participation, trained research assistants queried each participant’s substance use in the past year or since last study visit (Lisdahl et al., 2018). Each drug class was individually reported. For the present analyses, a binary yes/no variable for self-reported use of any type of cannabis product was coded. Additionally, total past year cannabis was calculated from those who used more than one standard unit. Total number of doses in the past year combined standard units as defined in Lisdahl et al. (2018) across all cannabis products queried (smoked flower, vaped, edible, dabs, combined cannabis and alcohol products, oils, and synthetic cannabinoids), which translates use into quantifiable amounts for most products (0.5 mg for a standard unit of cannabis flower; 1 mL cannabis infused oils; 1 g synthetic cannabinoids) or, for some, number of use episodes (cannabis concentrates).
Hair sample Collection, Selection, and analysis.
All participants with hairstyles that would not be disrupted by hair collection were asked to allow trained research assistants to carefully collect 100 mg hair (typically in 3–4 small undetectable snips at the root from the crown of their head). Hair was packaged and stored for future analysis. Due to financial limitations restricting analysis to a subsample of participants, hair analysis was selected for youth (1) who reported past-year cannabis use, (2) with elevated likelihood of substance use, or (3) were in a pool of participants considered unlikely to initiate use were randomly selected (approximately 10%; details available in (Wade et al., 2023; Wade et al., 2022).
Hair was securely stored at room temperature and shipped to Psychemedics (Culver City, CA) for analysis, previously described in detail elsewhere (Hill et al., 2016; Wade et al., 2023). Hair underwent a thorough wash procedure to mitigate environmental exposure to cannabis through smoke containing THC or CBD (Hill et al., 2014; Hill et al., 2016); THCCOOH, as the primary metabolite of THC, indicates definitive evidence of personal cannabis use rather than environmental exposure. THCCOOH was screened by immunoassay prior to testing by LC-MS/MS regardless of screening results, while other cannabinoids were tested directly by GC–MS/MS without screening. Samples were tested to the limit of detection to maximize sensitivity (THCCOOH, LOD/LOQ = 0.02 pg/mg; THC and CBD = 5 pg/mg). Up to 1.5 in of hair closest to the scalp were tested, providing a window of cannabinoid detection of up to 3-months. Individuals with shorter hair length had shorter detection windows; in the present analysis set, the shortest samples for a few participants reflected a 1.5-month window of detection and several had between 2 and 3-months, and the rest (n = 239) had samples facilitating a 3-month window. Only 225 of the 601 participants with hair samples at Year 4 Follow-Up had multiple instances of hair testing, sometime between Baseline and Year 3; 67 of CU youth have multiple instances of hair testing across one or more of the four prior time points of data collection.
Neurocognition
Neurocognitive performance was measured using the NIH Toolbox (Luciana et al., 2018; Weintraub et al., 2013). Tasks were administered by trained research assistants on 3rd generation iPad Air devices (10.5in). Six tasks were administered: (1) Picture Sequence Memory Test (“Picture Memory”)—a measure of episodic memory where participants are shown a sequence of images, which they recall in order (n = 241); (2) Picture Vocabulary Test—a measure of receptive language and estimated IQ where participants hear a word and are asked which of four pictures match the definition of that word (n = 242); (3) List Sorting Working Memory Test (“List Sort”)—a measure of working memory where participants sort stimuli presented both audibly and visually from smallest to largest (n = 242); (4) Flanker Inhibitory Control and Attention Test (“Flanker”)—a measure of attention and inhibition where participants respond to a central target stimuli in the middle of a row of either congruent or distracting stimuli (n = 238); (5) Pattern Comparison Process Speed Test (“Pattern Comparison”)—a measure of processing speed where participants quickly indicate whether two images are identical on as many items as possible within 90 s (n = 238); (6) Oral Reading Test—a measure of academic achievement where participants are asked to correctly read aloud and pronounce words (n = 242). Given the expected relatively large performance improvements across the participant age range (ages 12–15), age-normed standard scores were used in the present analyses.
Statistical analysis
All data analyses were completed in R version 4.1.0 (R Core Team, 2021) via RStudio (RStudio Team, 2021) utilizing 4 Year follow-up data from the ABCD Study. Neurocognitive data were checked for outliers via the outliers package (Komsta, 2022) using the Grubbs test; there were no outliers. Participants with missing data in a cognitive domain were excluded from analyses on that task.
Primary analysis.
Nested ANCOVA models were run using lme4 (Bates et al., 2015). Random effects of unique family identification codes (i.e., family relationship) were included, as the sample includes some sibling pairs. Maximally complex models (nested ANCOVAs) were attempted for all tests (Barr et al., 2013), with cognitive performance predicted by group status and nested family relationships. In some instances (i.e., Picture Memory, Pattern Comparison), nested ANCOVA models experienced an error of singularity due to overfitting; in these cases, standard ANCOVAs (i.e., non-nested) were run with cognitive performance on each impacted task predicted by group status, and family relationships included as a first level covariate.
Follow-Up analysis.
To assess dose-dependent relationships between cannabinoid hair content (THCCOOH, THC and CBD) and past-year cannabis use with cognitive performance, Pearson correlations were run within the CU group only, including those with cannabinoids in hair and/or self-reported cannabis use (n = 123).
Results
Sociodemographics and cannabis use.
As participants were matched on sociodemographics, groups did not differ on these characteristics. Participants were, on average, 14.3 years old (12.8–15.8 years old; SD = 0.7 years) and balanced on sex (48% female). Within the CU group, past-year self-reported cannabis doses marginally correlated with THCCOOH concentration (r(121) = 0.22, p = .06; see Fig. 1). Full sociodemographic characteristics are presented in Table 1, and cannabis use characteristics are in Table 2.
Cannabis use group analysis of neurocognition.
The CU group scored significantly lower on Picture Memory (F (1,238) = 4.67, partial η2 = 0.02, p = .03) and marginally lower on Picture Vocabulary (b = −0.23, partial R2 = 0.01, 95 % CI[−0.48,0.02]), p = .07) than the Control group. The CU group scored nearly 5 points (or ~⅓ of a standard deviation) lower on the Picture Memory task than Controls, on average (see Fig. 2). Though cannabis use status at Baseline (ages 9–10) cannot be confirmed through the same methods (e.g., hair analysis), performance on these tasks did not differ by group at Baseline (descriptive data can be viewed in the Supplement).
Cannabinoid concentrations in hair and neurocognition.
Within the CU group, higher THCCOOH concentrations were significantly associated with lower Picture Vocabulary (r(118) = −0.20, p = .03; see Fig. 3a) and Flanker (r(115) = −0.19, p = .04; see Fig. 3b) performance. Picture Memory performance was marginally negatively correlated with THCCOOH (r(117) = −0.18, p = .05). No correlations with THC or CBD hair test results were evident.
Past-Year cannabis use and neurocognition.
Within the CU group, greater self-reported past-year cannabis use was significantly associated with lower Picture Memory (r(117) = −0.19, p = .04,) and List Sort (r(118) = −0.33, p = .0002) performance.
Discussion
Adolescent cannabis use and cognitive performance have previously been related (Infante et al., 2020; Jacobus et al., 2019; Jacobus et al., 2015; Lisdahl & Price, 2012; Lisdahl et al., 2014; Wade et al., 2020). However, cannabis products are changing in cannabinoid content, and the relationship between cannabis and cognition in younger adolescents is less characterized. Here we identified youth who used cannabis through hair toxicology and self-report (CU), comparing their cognitive performance on the NIH Toolbox to that of matched controls. In a cross-sectional comparison of sociodemographically-matched CU youth to controls, the CU group performed more poorly on an episodic memory task and, marginally, on a receptive language task. Follow-up correlation analyses indicate that higher THCCOOH concentrations were associated with poorer language and attention performance. Self-reported past-year cannabis doses were also associated with lower performance on episodic and working memory tasks. Together, relationships between neurocognition and cannabis use in young adolescents (average age = 14) were seen in select cognitive domains. Investigating cannabis-cognition relationships requires sensitive metrics to ensure accurate identification of cannabis use, and biosamples such as hair toxicology may help optimally accomplish this in youth.
The present results mirror other cross-sectional studies of youth who have and have not used cannabis, yet here we investigated younger youth and lighter use patterns than most prior work. Cannabis use was long associated with cognitive deficits (Lees et al., 2021; Lisdahl et al., 2014; Lorenzetti et al., 2020; Mashhoon et al., 2019), specifically in episodic memory (Duperrouzel et al., 2019; Lawn et al., 2022; Medina et al., 2007), working memory (Hanson et al., 2010), and attention (Jacobus et al., 2015; Wallace et al., 2019). Importantly, the CU group scored, on average, 5 points (1/3 SD) lower than the Control group on a test of episodic memory (Picture Memory), consistent with prior research on cannabis-cognition relationships which found a 1/3rd standard deviation difference in those who used cannabis (Scott et al., 2019). As a cross-sectional study, the present cognitive performance differences might predate cannabis use initiation. As hair toxicology results indicate under-reporting of cannabis use (Wade et al., 2023; Wade et al., 2022) and repeat hair testing is limited in the current ABCD data release, we were not able to establish a time prior to initiation. However, here Baseline cognitive performance did not differ between groups and previous work in this cohort suggests that cognition is not a significant predictor of cannabis onset in early adolescence (Miller et al., 2023). Admittedly, that study relied solely on self-report when grouping youth with cannabis use. Other studies find cognition changes longitudinally post-initiation of cannabis use (Ajmera et al., 2021; Infante et al., 2020; Meier et al., 2012). Alternatively, other shared confounds may contribute to both cannabis use and lower cognition or lower cognitive performance may precede and predict cannabis initiation (Meier et al., 2018; Pope et al., 2003).
